papers.title: Reconfigurable Microwave Photonic All-Pass Filters based on Optical Kerr Microcombs
papers.label: arXiv:2611.29115v1

summary.one_liner: The paper demonstrates microwave photonic all-pass filters (1st and 2nd order) built from an optical Kerr microcomb driven transversal filter, with reconfiguration done by changing tap coefficients in software rather than hardware.
summary.plain: The paper is about filters that change the timing (phase) of radio-frequency signals without making them louder or quieter. The authors build such filters using light from a special optical comb, and they report measured results for first- and second-order versions. They also show the filter's behavior can be adjusted by changing settings in software, without rebuilding the hardware.
summary.why: Phase control of high-bandwidth microwave signals matters for radar and communications signal processing, so a reconfigurable way to build these filters could be useful. The text reports measured figures, but it does not compare them with other systems, so its standing relative to existing approaches cannot be judged from this text alone.
summary.background:
- All-pass filter: a filter that leaves signal strength unchanged and only shifts its phase (timing of the wave).
- Group delay: how much a signal's envelope is delayed by the filter; larger values mean stronger timing shifts.
- Microwave photonics: processing radio-frequency signals using light, then converting back to electronics.
- Optical Kerr microcomb: a set of evenly spaced optical frequencies (colors) generated in a micro-resonator through a nonlinear optical effect.
- Transversal filter: a filter that sums delayed, weighted copies of a signal; the weights are the "tap coefficients."
- Order of a filter: roughly how many independent phase-shifting stages it has; higher order gives more phase shift.
- Reported metrics: maximum amplitude variation (MAV, ripple in signal strength in dB) and maximum group delay (MGD, in picoseconds).

papers.abstract: Microwave photonic (MWP) all pass filters (APFs), which enable phase manipulation without altering signal amplitudes, are essential for phase engineering in high bandwidth microwave signal processing. However, achieving a high degree of reconfigurability in the filter order and characteristic parameters of APFs remains challenging for conventional methods. Here, we propose and experimentally demonstrate a new strategy for realizing MWP APFs based on a microcomb driven transversal filter system, enabling high reconfigurability, sharp phase transitions with high group delays, and low loss. We experimentally demonstrate both 1st and 2nd order APFs, achieving a maximum amplitude variation (MAV) of 1.95 dB and a maximum group delay (MGD) of 580 ps for the former, and a MAV of 2.01 dB and an MGD of 1740 ps for the latter. In addition, both independent and joint tuning of APF characteristic parameters are demonstrated by simply programming the tap coefficients without changing any hardware, enabling highly reconfigurable filter response for diverse phase engineering functionalities. These results highlight the potential of our approach for implementing MWP APFs with both high performance and reconfigurability for practical applications requiring dynamic and versatile phase control.

papers.title: Anisoplanatic Blind Deconvolution using Phase Diversity
papers.label: arXiv:2611.28458v1

summary.one_liner: A simulation study proposing coded anisoplanatic blind deconvolution (CA-BD), which uses a pupil-plane spatial light modulator to apply known phase codes across short measurement bursts to jointly recover a scene and spatially varying atmospheric phase, compared against tuned multiframe blind deconvolution.
summary.plain: Air turbulence bends light from distant objects, so images of stars or ground targets come out blurry, and the blur differs from one part of the view to another and changes over time. This paper proposes a way to undo that blur during fast imaging by placing a programmable light-modifying device in the optical path that applies a known pattern to each frame. In simulations, the method estimated the phase distortion more accurately than a tuned existing approach, with the authors reporting about 3.5 times lower phase error for steady turbulence and 2 to 3 times lower for changing turbulence.
summary.why: Turbulence blur limits telescopes and long-range cameras, and the paper targets the case where a wide field and fast imaging make standard computational deblurring fall short. The results are from simulation only, and the text notes the benefit depends on faster modulators, so practical impact is uncertain until hardware tests are reported.
summary.background:
- Atmospheric turbulence: random variations in air density that distort light wavefronts, blurring images.
- Isoplanatic angle: the angular range over which the distortion can be treated as the same; wider fields see different distortions.
- Phase / wavefront: the shape of the light wave's peaks; distortions here are phase errors.
- Blind deconvolution: recovering a sharp image when the blurring function is unknown, using multiple frames.
- Phase diversity: taking measurements with known, different phase patterns so the unknowns can be separated.
- Spatial light modulator (SLM): a programmable device that changes the phase of light pixel by pixel.
- Cramér-Rao bound: a theoretical lower limit on how precisely a quantity can be estimated.
- Coherence time: how long the turbulence stays roughly unchanged.

papers.abstract: Atmospheric turbulence distorts the wavefront of light from a distant scene and blurs its image. Over a field of view wider than the isoplanatic angle, the distortion varies with direction and evolves in time, so no single wavefront describes the blur. Multiframe blind deconvolution (MFBD) can recover the scene from measurements spread over a long acquisition, but falls short during fast imaging because of limited diversity across measurements. We present coded anisoplanatic blind deconvolution (CA-BD), in which a pupil-plane spatial light modulator (SLM) applies a different known phase code to every measurement, with no wavefront sensor or deformable mirror, so that the measurements carry diversity even within a short acquisition. A per-pixel single-layer estimator recovers the object and spatially varying phases from the coded measurements. In simulation, a Cram\'er-Rao bound analysis shows that under anisoplanatism direct imaging needs about 41 times the photons of coded imaging for equal phase precision in strong turbulence. At the stronger of two turbulence strengths, CA-BD outperforms tuned MFBD on average at every burst length. It reduces the phase mean squared error 3.5x for stationary turbulence and 2-3x for time-varying turbulence. Measurements taken within a few coherence times benefit most from the known coded SLM patterns, making faster SLMs the key to its full advantage in time-varying turbulence.

papers.title: Stellar Temporal Intensity Interferometry with Adaptive Optics at the Palomar Observatory
papers.label: arXiv:2611.30257v1

summary.background:
- Photon bunching: photons from thermal sources like stars tend to arrive in clumps; g^(2)(0) measures the strength of this clumping at zero time delay (1 means no correlation, higher means more bunching).
- Intensity interferometry: combining light intensity fluctuations from two telescopes (rather than raw light waves) to measure a star's angular size; it is robust to air turbulence.
- Temporal vs spatial correlation: spatial intensity interferometry compares light between separated telescopes; temporal version compares arrival times of photons at one detector.
- Adaptive optics: deformable mirrors that cancel out atmospheric blurring in real time.
- Narrowband spectral filtering: restricting light to a very narrow color band so the quantum correlation is not washed out.
- Single-photon counting: detectors that register individual photons and their arrival times.
- Red supergiant: a very large, cool, luminous star near the end of its life.
summary.one_liner: The paper reports the first detection of temporal photon bunching (a correlation in photon arrival times, quantified by g^(2)(0)) from a resolved star, α Her, using narrowband filtering, fast single-photon counters, and the adaptive optics system at Palomar Observatory.
summary.plain: Starlight arrives as a stream of individual light particles, and their arrival times can be correlated in a way that depends on the star's size and on quantum statistics. The authors looked for this timing pattern in light from the red supergiant α Her, using a very narrow color filter, fast photon detectors, and the telescope's adaptive optics, which corrects for air turbulence. They report a peak correlation value of 1.3 ± 0.1 for this star.
summary.why: The text claims this shows temporal intensity interferometry can be a practical observing method, linking quantum optics with stellar astronomy. Whether it will yield stellar measurements beyond this one target is not shown in the text, so its broader reach remains uncertain.

papers.abstract: Spatial intensity interferometry has seen a major resurgence in astronomy due to its immunity to atmospheric phase turbulence, but its temporal counterpart - a cornerstone of quantum optics - has remained largely unexplored for astronomical sources. Here, we demonstrate that high-visibility temporal photon bunching signatures from stellar sources are now accessible by combining ultra-narrowband spectral filtering with high-speed single-photon counting detectors. Leveraging the adaptive optics architecture at the Palomar Observatory, we report the first observation of resolved stellar temporal photon bunching, with a peak of $g^{(2)}(\tau=0) = 1.3 \pm 0.1$, from the red supergiant $\alpha$ Her. This advance establishes stellar temporal intensity interferometry as a viable observational modality, bridging quantum optics with high-resolution stellar astrophysics.

papers.title: 1.2 dB Insertion Loss in a Monolithically Integrated Silicon Mach-Zehnder Optical Isolator Using Stoichiometric Ce:YIG
papers.label: arXiv:2611.30501v1

summary.background:
- Optical isolator: a one-way valve for light; it stops back-reflected light from disturbing a laser or circuit.
- Photonic integrated circuit (PIC): a chip that guides light through tiny waveguides, analogous to an electronic chip for light.
- Magneto-optical (MO) effect: a material rotates the polarization of light when a magnetic field is applied; this rotation is what enables one-way behavior.
- Faraday rotation: the amount of polarization rotation per unit length; measured in degrees per centimeter.
- Figure of merit (FoM) here: Faraday rotation divided by optical loss, in degrees per dB; higher means less loss for a given rotation.
- Stoichiometry: the exact ratio of elements in a compound; deviations can form unwanted clusters.
- Ce:YIG: cerium-substituted yttrium iron garnet, a magneto-optical garnet material.
- Mach-Zehnder interferometer (MZI): a light-splitting and recombining layout used here to build the isolator.
- Insertion loss (dB) and isolation ratio (dB): how much light is lost passing forward, and how strongly backward light is blocked.
summary.one_liner: Shows that making cerium-doped yttrium iron garnet (Ce:YIG) films closer to exact stoichiometry, via an iron-deficient sputtering target, removes nano-cluster defects and yields a silicon Mach-Zehnder optical isolator with 1.2 dB insertion loss at 1556 nm.
summary.plain: Optical isolators are devices that let light pass in one direction while blocking reflections going back, which keeps chip-based light circuits stable. This paper addresses why such isolators on silicon chips lose too much light, and traces the problem to the chemical makeup of the magnetic garnet film used in them. By adjusting the target material so the film has the intended chemical ratio, the authors removed small clusters of mismatched material and built an isolator that lost only 1.2 dB of light.
summary.why: Insertion loss is a main obstacle to putting isolators on photonic chips, so a lower loss figure matters for that goal. The text reports a figure of merit 1.7 times higher than non-stoichiometric films, but it describes a single device demonstration, so its broader practical impact is not yet shown.

papers.abstract: Integrated optical isolators play a crucial role in photonic integrated circuits (PICs) by effectively stabilizing optical signals, making them indispensable components for advanced photonic systems. However, integrated magneto-optical (MO) isolators suffer from their high insertion loss, which is mainly caused by the relatively low FoM of Ce:YIG MO thin films deposited on silicon. Here, we show that film stoichiometry plays a key role in controlling the FoM of Ce:YIG. We observed garnet phase Fe-rich and Ce-rich nano-clusters in non-stoichiometric Ce:YIG. By using an iron-deficient target, we demonstrated that nearly stoichiometric Ce:YIG films on Si(100) could be fabricated, eliminating the nano-cluster defects. Consequently, the film exhibited a saturation Faraday rotation angle of -5523 deg/cm and a figure of merit of 72.7 deg/dB, which is 1.7 times higher compared to nonstoichiometric films. An MZI-type optical isolator on SiN fabricated by this method demonstrated a record low insertion loss of 1.2 dB and isolation ratio of 27.6 dB at 1556 nm wavelength. Our results provide an important step toward the practical application of integrated MO nonreciprocal photonic devices.

papers.title: Coherence Lengths of Laser Pointers
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26878v1

summary.background:
- Coherence length: the distance over which a light wave stays in step with itself; longer means more spectrally pure light.
- Interferometer: an instrument that splits a beam, recombines it, and reads the bright and dark fringes formed by the overlap.
- Noncollinear beam geometry: the two beams cross at an angle rather than travelling along the same line.
- Multimodal behavior: a laser emitting several slightly different wavelengths (modes) at once, which shortens coherence length.
- Diode laser and diode-pumped solid-state (DPSS) laser: two common designs; the green pointer uses a solid-state crystal that doubles an infrared neodymium laser's frequency to green.
- CMOS detector array: the same kind of sensor chip found in cameras, used here to record the fringe pattern.
summary.one_liner: The paper measures the coherence lengths of several low-cost green laser pointers, using a noncollinear-beam interferometer read out by a CMOS detector array, and finds values that can exceed 10 cm while varying from device to device.
summary.plain: Coherence length is how far a light beam can travel and still interfere with a copy of itself, a rough measure of how "pure" or single-colored the light is. The authors tested cheap green laser pointers, including three diode-type lasers and one frequency-doubled solid-state laser, to see how far their light stayed coherent. They found the answer varies between devices, but often reaches more than 10 cm.
summary.why: The work is modest in scope: it characterizes everyday consumer lasers and suggests the setup could serve as a teaching experiment for advanced undergraduates. The abstract also says it may inspire laser-pointer designs that rely on interference, but that is speculative and not demonstrated in the text.

papers.abstract: We report on the coherence lengths of low-cost green laser pointers in the midst of multimodal behavior using an optical interferometer based on noncollinear beam geometries and a CMOS detector array. Examined devices include three diode lasers and a frequency-doubled neodymium-emission diode-pumped solid state (DPSS) laser. Coherence length measurements are variable among devices, but values can nevertheless regularly exceed 10 cm. The work serves as a template for an advanced undergraduate physics laboratory experiment and may inspire new kinds of laser pointer devices utilizing interference effects as operative principles.

papers.title: Test of gravitational redshift by optical clocks at different latitudes
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27588v1

summary.background:
- General relativity: Einstein's theory of gravity, which says gravity affects the passage of time.
- Gravitational redshift: clocks lower in a gravitational field run slower compared with clocks higher up; the shift is seen as a change in frequency.
- Optical atomic clocks: very precise clocks that count the oscillations of light absorbed by atoms, far more stable than ordinary clocks.
- Geodetic measurements: precise surveys of the heights and positions of the clock sites relative to Earth's shape.
- Centrifugal potential: the effective pull from Earth's spin, which depends on latitude and partly cancels gravity's height effect.
- Uncertainty level: the size of the largest plausible error; smaller means a stricter test.
summary.one_liner: Two Earth-fixed optical atomic clocks at different latitudes are compared against the gravitational redshift predicted by general relativity, using independent geodetic height data, reaching a 4.6×10^-5 uncertainty and arguing that Earth's rotation can enhance sensitivity to a violation.
summary.plain: The paper checks a prediction of Einstein's general relativity: clocks sitting higher in a gravitational field tick slightly faster. The authors compared the ticking of two optical atomic clocks placed at different heights and latitudes on Earth, and found the measured difference matches the predicted shift. Their main new idea is that separating the clocks north-south, not just up-down, can make the test more sensitive because Earth's rotation partly offsets the height difference.
summary.why: The result tightens ground-based tests of a basic relativity prediction by about a factor of two, according to the text, and the latitude approach is presented as a new way to get closer to space-based test sensitivity. Its wider significance beyond precision testing of relativity is not stated in the text.

papers.abstract: General relativity predicts that frequency comparisons between clocks are affected by both gravitational and kinematic time dilation. While the kinematic contribution has been tested with high accuracy, experimental tests of the gravitational redshift remain comparatively less stringent. Here, we measure the frequency shift between two Earth-fixed optical atomic clocks at different potentials and compare it to the redshift predicted by general relativity using independent geodetic measurements. The observed shift agrees with the prediction, testing the gravitational redshift at the $4.6 \times 10^{-5}$ uncertainty level, improving ground-based tests by a factor two. Previous ground-based tests separated the clocks mainly vertically. For clocks at different latitudes, their height difference is governed not only by the gravitational potentials at their locations but also by the centrifugal potentials caused by Earth's rotation. As both contributions can partially cancel, the gravitational contribution can be considerably larger than their height difference suggests. In this work, a separation of the clocks by $4^\circ$ in latitude enhances their sensitivity to a gravitational redshift violation threefold, to the equivalent of an approximately 1200 m difference in height for small latitudinal separation. Our results establish Earth's rotation as a so far unexploited resource for advancing ground-based tests of the gravitational redshift towards the sensitivity of previous space-based experiments.

papers.title: Fast electrons and high energy photons produced in strong-field ionization of atoms as diagnostics of multi-petawatt laser beams
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26496v1

summary.background:
- Tunnel ionization: in a very strong laser field, the electric field bends the atom's binding barrier so an electron can leak out of the atom.
- Petawatt: one quadrillion watts of power, though the pulse lasts only a very short time.
- Peak intensity: the power concentrated per unit area at the focus, which sets how strongly the atoms are driven.
- Focal spot field configuration: the shape and structure of the electric field in the small region where the beam is focused, which is not uniform.
- Polarization: the direction in which the laser's electric field oscillates.
- Photoelectrons and X-ray photons: electrons and light quanta emitted by the atom during ionization; higher-energy photons are X-rays.
- The work is numerical (computer simulation), not an experiment.
summary.one_liner: Numerical calculations of photoelectron and X-ray photon spectra and angular distributions from tunnel ionization of argon in multi-petawatt focused laser fields, showing sensitivity to peak intensity and focal-spot field configuration.
summary.plain: This paper looks at how to measure how intense a very powerful laser beam is, by watching the fast electrons and high-energy X-ray photons that the laser knocks out of argon atoms. The authors simulated these emissions for laser powers in the multi-petawatt range, varying the power, how tightly the beam is focused, and its polarization. They report that the energies and directions of the emitted particles change with these settings, so they could in principle serve as a diagnostic.
summary.why: Multi-petawatt lasers are newly built facilities, and their peak intensity is hard to measure directly at the focus, so a reliable diagnostic would be useful to those facilities. The text says the findings agree with earlier proposals, but it does not report any experimental test, so the practical reliability remains to be shown.

papers.abstract: We calculate numerically energy spectra and angular distributions of photoelectrons and X-ray photons emitted in the process of tunnel photoionization of argon by a focused laser beam of multi-petawatt power. By scanning the beam power and varying the degree of focusing and the field polarization, we show these distributions to be sensitive both to the peak laser intensity and to the field configuration in the focal spot. Investigated parameters of the laser beam correspond to those of several recently commissioned lasers of multi-petawatt power. These findings, in line with the earlier reported proposals, provide a basis for the development of a reliable ionization diagnostics of extremely intense laser fields.

papers.title: Dephasing-free plasma acceleration with millijoule picosecond lasers
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26032v1

summary.background:
- Laser-plasma acceleration: a laser pulse creates a wave in a plasma that can carry and accelerate electrons, reaching gradients far above conventional radio-frequency cavities.
- Dephasing: accelerated electrons eventually outrun the wave that is accelerating them, which limits the energy gain.
- Plasma frequency: the natural oscillation rate of electrons in a plasma; here laser colors are spaced by this amount.
- Particle-in-cell (PIC) simulation: a computer method that tracks particles and fields together; the results here come from such simulations.
- Manley–Rowe limit: a physical bound on how much laser energy can be converted into the plasma wave, given the photon energies involved.
- Units: GV/m is accelerating gradient (energy gained per meter); MeV is an energy unit; mJ and ps are millijoules and picoseconds.
summary.one_liner: A proposed laser-plasma accelerator driven by a comb of laser lines spaced at the plasma frequency, each in its own mode of a matched channel, reports simulated gradients of about 21 GV/m with millijoule-to-175 mJ picosecond drives and reduced dephasing.
summary.plain: Particle accelerators usually need very large, expensive lasers to push electrons to high energy inside a plasma, a hot gas of charged particles. This paper proposes a way to do this with much less laser energy, using a set of closely spaced laser colors that build up a wave in the plasma that keeps pace with the electrons. In computer simulations only, the authors report accelerating test electrons to about 170 to 208 MeV with drives as small as 10 to 175 millijoules.
summary.why: If the simulated results hold up in experiments, laser-driven accelerators could become far cheaper and run at higher repetition rates, which would matter for compact accelerator applications. The text presents only simulation results, so practical feasibility is unverified.

papers.abstract: Laser-plasma accelerators reach gradients a thousand times above radio-frequency cavities, but need joule-class femtosecond lasers firing about once per second, and electrons outrun the wave. A comb of laser lines spaced by the plasma frequency, each in its own mode of a matched channel, drives a wake moving at the speed of light. In particle-in-cell simulations a 175\,mJ, 0.5\,ps drive holds 21\,GV/m over 10\,mm with a 0.15\,rad phase drift; a test electron gains 208\,MeV, 2.6 times more than in one mode. Because the wave builds up resonantly, the required energy falls steeply with density: a 29\,mJ drive sustains 20\,GV/m, and a 10\,mJ drive, within reach of kilohertz industrial lasers, gives a test electron 170\,MeV over 30\,mm. A simulated stage transfers 5\,\% of the laser energy to the wake; the Manley--Rowe limit is about 18\,\% for five lines.

papers.title: Delay Mismatches Shape the Spectra of Three Synchronized Semiconductor Lasers
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24306v1

summary.background:
- Chaotic laser: a laser whose output brightness fluctuates irregularly, not in a steady or simply periodic way.
- Synchronization: coupled systems whose irregular signals end up matching each other in time.
- Delay (time lag): light takes a finite time to travel between lasers or back from a feedback mirror, so each link has a delay; a delay mismatch is a difference between these times.
- Radio-frequency spectrum: a breakdown of a signal's brightness fluctuations by how fast they oscillate, showing which frequencies are strongest.
- Harmonics: whole-number multiples of a base frequency; overlapping harmonics from different links can reinforce each other and create peaks.
summary.one_liner: Experiments and numerical simulations of three mutually coupled chaotic semiconductor lasers show that small mismatches in their coupling and feedback delay times set the characteristic frequencies and peak structure of the synchronized intensity spectra.
summary.plain: This paper looks at three lasers that are linked together so that their chaotic flickering in brightness falls into step with one another. The researchers measured the radio-frequency spectrum of that flickering, meaning which rates of fluctuation carry the most power. They found that the peaks depend on which lasers are synchronized and on tiny differences in the time delays between them, and simulations with the same delays matched the measured peak positions and overall shape.
summary.why: The text suggests a simple rule: peaks appear where several harmonic contributions line up in frequency, and the inverse of each delay mismatch sets a characteristic frequency. This may be useful for predicting or controlling the spectra of networks of coupled lasers, but the text does not say which applications it would affect.

papers.abstract: We study a network of three synchronized chaotic lasers and the radio frequency spectra of the intensity fluctuations. The position and morphology of the peaks are significantly different depending on the set of lasers being synchronized. The lasers and coupling paths are similar but not identical in all parameters, including their feedback and coupling delay times. The inverse of the delay mismatch between each pair of lasers introduces characteristic frequencies that shape the spectral response of the synchronized system. By studying two different three-laser configurations, we find that peaks appear whenever multiple harmonic contributions overlap in frequency, resulting in constructive enhancement of the spectral power. Numerical simulations performed with the same delay configurations show a clear agreement with the experimental measurements, reproducing both the peak positions and the overall spectral structure. These results indicate that the frequency content of the synchronized dynamics is largely determined by the delay-mismatch network and its harmonics.

papers.title: Squeezed Cooling and Lasing with Cold Atoms in Cavity-QED
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24743v1

summary.background:
- Squeezed light: light whose noise is reduced in one measurable direction (a quadrature) below the vacuum noise floor, with extra noise in the conjugate direction.
- Optical cavity: two mirrors that trap light so it bounces back and forth and interacts repeatedly with atoms.
- Cold atoms: atoms cooled by lasers to very low temperatures, so they can be controlled precisely.
- Raman transition: a two-photon process that moves an atom between energy levels, here assisted by the cavity.
- Lasing threshold: the pumping level at which stimulated emission overtakes losses and a coherent beam appears.
- Coherence time and linewidth: how long a light wave stays in a stable phase, and how narrow its frequency spread is.
- Optical parametric oscillator (OPO): the standard nonlinear-crystal device for making squeezed light; the text cites its 3 dB limit for intracavity squeezing.
- Decibel (dB): a logarithmic scale for noise reduction; 3 dB is roughly halving the noise power.
summary.one_liner: A theoretical proposal for a squeezed laser built from cold rubidium atoms coupled to a squeezed cavity mode via cavity-assisted Raman transitions, using "squeezed cooling" to prepare squeezed light without a nonlinear crystal or injected squeezed light.
summary.plain: Light can be "squeezed," meaning the uncertainty in one of its two measurable properties is reduced below the normal background noise, at the cost of more noise in the other. This paper proposes a way to produce such light using clouds of cold rubidium atoms inside an optical cavity, instead of the usual nonlinear crystals. The authors report, from their modeling, that one atom ensemble can cool the cavity into a squeezed state, and a second pumped ensemble can produce a laser beam whose noise stays below the vacuum level over a band about a megahertz wide.
summary.why: Squeezed light is used in precision measurements such as gravitational-wave detectors, so a route that avoids crystals could matter for that kind of work. The text is a proposal and modeling study, and it does not show that the scheme has been built or tested, so its practical value is still uncertain.

papers.abstract: A squeezed laser undergoes a lasing transition into a squeezed cavity mode, where stimulated emission generates a bright coherent field with a laser-like coherence time while maintaining one field quadrature below the vacuum noise level. Here we propose an optical implementation that needs neither a nonlinear crystal nor injected squeezed light, based on engineered interactions between ensembles of rubidium atoms and a squeezed cavity mode via cavity-assisted Raman transitions. A first ensemble cools the cavity into a squeezed vacuum, a mechanism we term squeezed cooling, yielding up to 9 dB in the intracavity field, surpassing the 3 dB limit of optical parametric oscillators. Tuned for output instead, it reaches up to 18 dB of output squeezing. Incoherently pumping a second ensemble drives a lasing transition into the squeezed mode, emitting a bright beam with long coherence time and noise below vacuum spanning a megahertz-wide band, away from the sharp phase-diffusion peak of excess noise at the carrier frequency, and robust to relaxation oscillations. We characterize lasing thresholds, superradiant emission, and linewidth narrowing, and identify the experimentally accessible regime where the system exhibits the defining features of a squeezed laser.

papers.title: Optical rectification and Pockels effect in the organic nonlinear crystal MBI for quasi-discrete THz time-domain spectroscopy
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22729v1

summary.background:
- Terahertz (THz) radiation: electromagnetic waves between microwave and infrared frequencies (1 THz is about 1 trillion cycles per second); used to study molecular vibrations and material properties.
- Optical rectification: a nonlinear optical effect in which a strong laser pulse in a crystal generates a THz pulse at low frequencies.
- Pockels effect: a change in a crystal's refractive index under an electric field; used here to detect THz pulses by how they alter a probe laser's polarization.
- Time-domain spectroscopy: measuring the THz electric field pulse over time, then computing its frequency spectrum.
- Telecom wavelength (~1.5 μm): the infrared band used in fiber-optic communications, where cheap, reliable lasers exist.
- MHz-rate femtosecond fiber laser: a laser emitting ultrashort pulses millions of times per second.
- Dynamic range (dB): the ratio between the strongest and weakest signals a measurement can distinguish; 40 dB is a factor of 10,000.
summary.one_liner: The paper reports terahertz (THz) generation and electro-optic detection in the organic nonlinear crystal MBI pumped by a 1.5 μm MHz-rate femtosecond fiber laser, yielding quasi-discrete emission spanning 1–30 THz with a prominent peak at 11.8 THz.
summary.plain: Terahertz light sits between microwaves and infrared light, and it is useful for probing materials by how they absorb it. This paper describes making and detecting this kind of light with a special organic crystal (MBI) driven by a telecom-wavelength laser, the same wavelength family used in fiber-optic internet equipment. The authors report that the crystal emits roughly 1 microwatt of THz light across a very wide range, and that a measurement with more than 40 dB of dynamic range can be done within minutes.
summary.why: Most strong THz sources need bulkier, more expensive lasers, so a crystal that works with inexpensive, high-repetition-rate fiber lasers could make THz spectroscopy more accessible. The text does not compare this against other sources or give application results, so the practical significance beyond the reported measurements is uncertain.

papers.abstract: Organic nonlinear optical (NLO) crystals offer efficient nonlinear frequency conversion for broadband THz spectroscopy. Unfortunately, only a subset of NLO crystals is compatible with the telecom (~1.5 $μ$m) pump wavelength region, where convenient MHz-rate femtosecond fiber lasers are available. Here, we present ultra-broadband (1-30 THz) THz generation and detection using a benzoindolium iodide (MBI, C$_{24}$H$_{24}$NOI) crystal illuminated by a 1.5 $μ$m MHz-rate fiber laser. At 200 mW of average pump power, the crystal delivers ~1 $μ$W of THz radiation as quasi-discrete peaks covering the whole emission region with a prominent peak at 11.8 THz. High-dynamic range (>40 dB) time-domain spectroscopy is demonstrated within minutes of integration.

papers.title: Microwave hinge states in an all-dielectric woodpile photonic crystal insulator
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22196v1

summary.background:
- Photonic crystal: a periodic structure whose repeating pattern blocks waves in certain frequency ranges, the way a crystal affects electrons.
- Photonic bandgap: a range of frequencies that cannot propagate through the structure in any direction.
- Topological insulator: a material that is an insulator in its bulk but supports protected edge or surface waves at its boundaries.
- Higher-order topology: a generalization in which protected states appear at lower-dimensional features, here hinges (edges where two surfaces meet), not just surfaces.
- Woodpile structure: a stack of crossing rods or layers forming a 3D lattice.
- Microwaves: electromagnetic waves with wavelengths of about a millimeter to a centimeter, which is why the lattice can be built at millimeter scale.
- Boundary polarization: a label describing how the material's charge-like response is arranged at a boundary; matching or mismatching labels determine whether a hinge state exists.
summary.one_liner: The paper reports experimental observation of higher-order topological hinge states, localized at intersections of two interfaces, in a millimeter-scale all-dielectric woodpile photonic crystal at microwave frequencies, and shows their absence at intersections where boundary polarizations are equivalent.
summary.plain: Researchers built a three-dimensional structure out of a non-metallic material that blocks microwaves in a full range of directions, somewhat like a crystal that blocks light. Where two special boundaries of this structure meet along an edge, the team found that microwaves can travel along that edge and stay trapped there. They also found that at other meeting points, where the boundaries are equivalent, no such edge-trapped wave appears, as the theory predicted.
summary.why: The work tests a theoretical prediction about a newer class of topological states, in which waves are confined to edges (hinges) rather than surfaces. It is worth attention as an experimental check of higher-order topology in three dimensions, though the text does not indicate specific applications.

papers.abstract: Higher-order topological states are studied in a woodpile photonic crystal (PhC) having a large complete photonic bandgap. According to theoretical predictions, we fabricate a three-dimensional all-dielectric PhC with a millimeter-scale lattice period. The structure consists of two distinct lattice types that coincide through a structural displacement, where their interface intersection gives rise to hinge states. Microwave transmission measurements reveal transmission peaks and spatial localization at the intersection, demonstrating the hinge states. Furthermore, we confirm the absence of hinge states at a specific intersection. As theoretically predicted, hinge states emerge at intersections where the localized boundary polarizations are topologically different, whereas they are absent at intersections where the boundary polarizations are equivalent.

papers.title: Fundamental physics with quantum sensors in space
papers.label: arXiv:2611.21997v1

summary.background:
- Quantum sensors: devices that use the behavior of individual atoms to measure time, acceleration, or magnetic fields very precisely.
- Atomic clock: a timekeeper based on the fixed oscillation frequency of atoms; extremely sensitive to tiny changes in gravity.
- Atom interferometer: splits a cloud of atoms along two paths and recombines them to measure gravity or acceleration from the pattern they form.
- Standard Model: the current best theory of particles and forces; dark matter and gravitational waves in some bands lie partly outside what it fully explains or what can be seen directly.
- General relativity: Einstein's theory of gravity as curved spacetime.
- Gravitational waves: ripples in spacetime from massive accelerating objects; low-frequency ones are hard to detect from Earth because of ground noise.
- Microgravity: the near-weightlessness found in orbit, which lets atoms be observed for longer.
- Proceedings: a collection of written papers from a scientific meeting.
summary.one_liner: Workshop proceedings surveying the scientific case, current capabilities, and mission concepts for using space-based quantum sensors (atomic clocks, atom interferometers, atomic magnetometers) to search for dark matter, test general relativity, and detect gravitational waves in bands hard to reach from the ground.
summary.plain: This is a set of proceedings from a 2026 physics workshop on using ultra-precise atomic instruments in space. The authors argue that space offers a quieter, weightless environment with long distances and varying gravity, which could help detect faint signals from unknown physics. The text is a summary of the case for these experiments and the mission ideas, not a report of new measurements.
summary.why: It maps out where space-based quantum sensing might probe dark matter, general relativity, and gravitational waves that ground experiments cannot reach. Whether these mission concepts become real depends on future funding and technical progress, which the summary does not assess.

papers.abstract: Quantum sensors such as atomic clocks, atom interferometers, and atomic magnetometers can be used as sensitive probes of physics beyond the Standard Model. Space offers microgravity, long baselines, low environmental noise, access to varying gravitational potentials, and unique opportunities involving the Sun, Moon, planets, and asteroids. These proceedings of the Aspen Center for Physics workshop on "Fundamental physics in space with quantum sensors," held February 22-27, 2026, summarize the scientific case, current capabilities, and space mission concepts for investigating dark matter, testing general relativity, and detecting gravitational waves in frequency bands inaccessible from the ground.

papers.title: Laser Processing for Energy Applications
papers.label: arXiv:2611.21024v1

summary.background:
- Laser: a beam of concentrated light; power and pulse length determine what it can do to a material.
- Inertial confinement fusion: fusion reactions triggered by squeezing a tiny fuel pellet with intense laser pulses so it heats and compresses for a very brief moment.
- Photovoltaic (solar) cell: a device that converts sunlight into electricity; laser processing can shape its surfaces or contacts.
- Concentrated solar power: uses mirrors to focus sunlight to produce heat, often for generating electricity.
- Surface texturing: deliberately creating tiny patterns or roughness on a material's surface to change how it interacts with liquids, light or electric charge.
- Lithium-ion battery: a rechargeable battery whose electrodes store and release lithium ions; manufacturing steps such as cutting or joining electrodes can use lasers.
- Electrochemical performance: how well a material stores or transfers charge in a battery or similar device.
summary.one_liner: A book chapter surveying laser applications across energy topics: laser-driven inertial confinement fusion, laser roles in solar cells and concentrated solar power, laser-based surface texturing for electrochemical performance, and laser techniques in lithium-ion battery materials and manufacturing.
summary.plain: This is an overview chapter, not a report of a single experiment. It describes how lasers are used in several energy areas: creating fusion energy by compressing fuel with intense light, improving and recycling solar panels, roughening or patterning surfaces to help electrodes work better, and making and improving lithium-ion batteries. The text summarizes these topics and ends with a look at future possibilities.
summary.why: Laser processing is a common tool in manufacturing, and energy technologies such as fusion, solar power and batteries all depend on it to varying degrees, so a survey can help readers see how these areas connect. The provided text is only the abstract-level summary, so it does not show specific new results or how strong the evidence is for each claim.

papers.abstract: Laser processing has emerged as a transformative technology in the energy sector, enabling precise, efficient, and scalable solutions for energy generation, storage, and sustainability. This chapter explores the diverse applications of laser technology in energy applications. It begins with an overview of laser-driven inertial confinement fusion for energy production, highlighting key experimental facilities and crucial laser parameters. The role of lasers in solar energy harvesting is examined, including photovoltaic cell optimization, concentrated solar power, and laser-assisted recycling of solar modules. The chapter further reviews recent developments into laser-based techniques for enhancing electrochemical performance through surface texturing at various scales. Advancements in lithium-ion battery technology are also discussed, focusing on next-generation materials, battery manufacturing processes, and the impact of laser techniques on performance, safety, and scalability. The chapter concludes with insights into future prospects for laser applications in sustainable energy solutions.
